newsitem.title: UK: Margins cut for IPE natgas, longer hours mulled.
newsitem.headline: Margins cut for IPE natgas, longer hours mulled.

text.p: A cut in margins is the first step to increasing liquidity on the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) natural gas futures contract and could be followed by further modifications such as longer trading hours, market players said on Thursday.
Futures brokers and physical gas traders met with IPE officials on Wednesday to discuss issues of liquidity.
A cut in margins from 3.50 pence per therm (p/th) to 3.00 p/th was announced by the London Clearing House (LCH), which said it planned to review margins on a monthly basis.
"It's encouraging that the LCH has made a change early and I think we can look forward to further decreases," said a trader for a major shipper.
Extending trading hours from the current two sessions of 1000 to 1200 and 1400 to 1600 London time, to a non-stop session from 1000 to 1700 was also on the agenda.
"I think this will go through," said one major shipper.
But demands by larger players to increase the minimum trade from five lots, or 5,000 therms a day, to 10 lots or 10,000 therms a day, were more contentious.

"There's a lot of sentiment among the bigger players for pushing the minimum trade size higher. You don't want to take out a big position if the price can be pushed around on very small volumes," one shipper said.
"Increasing the trading size would be the best step towards increasing liquidity," he added.
But some brokers said this would be a barrier to entry and argued for a minimum trades of just one lot to encourage smaller players into the market.
Proposals to double the tick size from 0.005 per contract to 0.01 and introduce strip trading across quarters received broad approval, said those attending the meeting.
"(The meeting) was very encouraging," said an IPE spokeswoman. "The working group was very open and there was a lot of compromising."
"The way to get volumes up is a very contentious issue at the moment... There's a lot of goodwill but no real action," said one floor broker.
